en.title: Computer Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What computer engineering covers, how degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What computer engineering is
sections.text:
Computer engineering is the design and study of computing systems as physical and logical machines. It joins electrical and electronic engineering with computer science: students learn circuits, signals and devices, and also software, algorithms and data. The work ranges from a single transistor or sensor to a microprocessor, a network of embedded devices, and the software that runs on them.

The subject matters because modern products depend on hardware and software working together under real constraints: speed, power, cost, safety and reliability. A computer engineer must be able to reason about both sides and test the whole system.

These summaries teach principles. They do not replace datasheets, standards, design codes or supervised practice. Rules for professional registration differ by country; in Nigeria the regulator is COREN, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria. Always check the current official source for your country and institution.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Degree names, lengths and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a BEng in Computer Engineering usually takes five years and includes industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnics usually offer an ND (National Diploma), then supervised industrial work, then an HND (Higher National Diploma). In England, Wales and Northern Ireland a BEng usually takes three years and an MEng four; Scottish degrees often take a year longer. Other countries have their own patterns.

The early years are usually shared with other engineering students: mathematics, physics, circuit theory, programming and digital logic. Later years add architecture, microprocessors, embedded systems, communications, control and design. Most programmes end with a design project, and professional practice or ethics is usually taught near the end. A master’s degree adds advanced architecture, hardware security, edge AI and research methods.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually begins with engineering mathematics: calculus and series, linear algebra and matrices, discrete mathematics, and probability and statistics. These support circuit theory for DC and AC networks, digital logic and number systems, programming in C, and semiconductor devices and diodes.

The core then builds upwards. Sequential logic and finite state machines lead into computer architecture and organisation, microprocessors and microcontrollers, assembly language and embedded programming. Analogue electronic circuits and operational amplifiers cover signal conditioning. Signals and systems lead to digital signal processing and control systems. Data communications and networking connect machines to each other.

Later core subjects include embedded systems design, digital system design with HDL (hardware description language) and FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays), VLSI (very large scale integration) fundamentals, real-time operating systems, professional practice and ethics, and the design project. In Nigeria, professional practice should cover COREN registration and the engineer’s legal and ethical duties. Master’s topics include advanced computer architecture, hardware security and trust, edge AI (machine learning on local devices) and embedded machine learning, and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study by doing. Work through problems by hand before using software, and build small circuits or programs where you can. For circuits, draw the schematic and label currents and voltages. For digital logic, write truth tables and timing diagrams. For programming, compile and test small programs, and read the compiler warnings.

Keep a laboratory notebook. Record what you expected, what happened and why. Learn to use a datasheet, an oscilloscope and a debugger. Ask whether a result is reasonable: a microcontroller pin cannot supply a heavy motor directly, and a signal cannot pass a filter unchanged at every frequency.

Revise in short, regular sessions. Explain a topic aloud or teach it to a classmate. Use past questions, but understand the method rather than memorising answers.

keyPoints: Computer engineering combines electronic hardware with software and computing systems.
Degree length and title vary by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Mathematics, circuits, programming and digital logic are the foundation for later core subjects.
Learn by solving problems by hand, building and testing small systems, and reading datasheets.

en.title: Engineering mathematics: calculus and series
en.short: Limits, derivatives, integrals, partial derivatives, Taylor and Fourier series, multiple integrals and ODEs.

sections.heading: Limits and derivatives
sections.text:
A limit is the value a function approaches as its input approaches a point. A derivative is the limit of a change quotient: f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)] ÷ h. It gives the instantaneous rate of change, such as velocity from displacement or current from charge.

For several variables, z = f(x,y), the partial derivative ∂z/∂x treats y as constant. The gradient vector (∂z/∂x, ∂z/∂y) points in the direction of steepest increase. Engineering uses these in optimisation and error analysis.

Example: f(x) = x². f′(x) = 2x, so at x = 3 the slope is 6.

sections.heading: Integration and partials
sections.text:
Integration reverses differentiation. A definite integral ∫ from a to b f(x) dx gives signed area; physically it can give work, charge or total change. For f(x)=x², ∫₀² x² dx = [x³/3]₀² = 8/3.

For several variables, a double integral ∬ f(x,y) dA adds a quantity over an area; a triple integral over a volume. Partial derivatives and multiple integrals appear in heat flow, stress and field calculations.

sections.heading: Taylor and Fourier
sections.text:
A Taylor series expands a function about a point as an infinite sum of powers: f(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x−a) + f″(a)(x−a)²/2! + ... . Truncating it gives an approximation, used in numerical methods and small-signal models.

A Fourier series writes a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines. It is central to signal processing and AC circuit analysis. Coefficients depend on the period and the waveform.

sections.heading: Multiple integrals and ODEs
sections.text:
Multiple integrals extend integration to two or three variables. An ordinary differential equation (ODE) relates a function to its derivatives. First-order ODEs are solved by separation of variables or an integrating factor; constant-coefficient second-order linear ODEs use characteristic equations. They model circuits, motion and cooling.

Example: dy/dx = 2x gives y = x² + C. If y(0)=1, then C=1, so y=x²+1.

keyPoints: Derivative: f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)] ÷ h.
Partial derivative ∂f/∂x treats other variables as constants; the gradient points to steepest increase.
Definite integral ∫ from a to b f(x) dx gives signed area or total change.
Taylor series: f(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x−a) + f″(a)(x−a)²/2! + ... .
Fourier series represents periodic functions as sums of sines and cosines.
First-order ODE dy/dx = g(x) can be solved by separation: y = ∫g(x)dx + C.

en.title: Linear algebra and matrices
en.short: Vectors, matrices, determinants, linear systems, eigenvalues, vector spaces and circuit applications.

sections.heading: Vectors and matrices
sections.text: A vector is a list of n numbers. A matrix is a rectangular array. Matrix addition and scalar multiplication work entry by entry. Matrix multiplication combines rows of the first with columns of the second, so AB generally differs from BA. The identity matrix I leaves a vector unchanged. The transpose swaps rows and columns. A square matrix is invertible when its determinant is not zero.

sections.heading: Determinants and systems
sections.text:
The determinant of a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]] is ad − bc. A nonzero determinant means the matrix has an inverse and Ax = b has one unique solution. Gaussian elimination reduces the system to triangular form by row operations. If a pivot is zero, swap rows. If a row reduces to 0 = 0, there are infinitely many solutions; if the left side becomes zero but the constant does not, there is no solution.

Example: 2x + y = 5 and x + 3y = 10. det = 2×3 − 1×1 = 5. By Cramer’s rule, x = (5×3 − 1×10) ÷ 5 = 1 and y = (2×10 − 5×1) ÷ 5 = 3. Check: 2(1)+3=5 and 1+3(3)=10.

sections.heading: Eigenvalues and spaces
sections.text: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector v that satisfies Av = λv for a square matrix A, where the scalar λ is its eigenvalue. Eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0. They describe directions unchanged by a linear transformation. A vector space is a set closed under addition and scalar multiplication. A basis is a smallest spanning set; its size is the dimension. Vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero. An orthogonal basis makes coordinates easy to find.

sections.heading: Circuits and transforms
sections.text: In circuit analysis, nodal equations have the form Gv = i, where G is a conductance matrix, v holds node voltages and i holds currents. Mesh equations have the form Ri = v. Solving these systems gives the unknown voltages or currents. Phasors turn steady AC quantities into complex numbers, so the same matrix methods apply. Fourier and Laplace transforms are linear: they turn derivatives into multiplication, converting differential circuit equations into algebraic ones.

keyPoints: Matrix multiplication is row by column and is not generally commutative.
For a 2×2 matrix, det = ad − bc; a nonzero determinant gives a unique solution to Ax = b.
Eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0 and eigenvectors satisfy Av = λv.
Orthogonal vectors have zero dot product; a basis spans the space with no redundancy.
Circuit laws give linear systems such as Gv = i and Ri = v.
Fourier and Laplace transforms are linear and turn derivatives into multiplication.

en.title: Discrete mathematics for computing
en.short: Logic, proof, sets, relations, functions, counting, graphs, trees and number theory for computing.

sections.heading: Logic and proof
sections.text:
Propositional logic builds statements from atomic propositions using AND, OR, NOT, implication (→) and equivalence (↔). A truth table lists all truth combinations. Predicate logic adds variables, predicates such as P(x), and quantifiers: ∀ means for all, ∃ means there exists. A proof is a valid argument from definitions and known results. Common methods are direct proof, proof by contradiction and induction, which proves a base case and an induction step.

Example: prove 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2. Base n=1: both sides equal 1. If true for n, add n+1: n(n+1)/2 + (n+1) = (n+1)(n+2)/2, the formula for n+1.

sections.heading: Sets and relations
sections.text: A set is a collection of objects. Operations include union, intersection, difference and complement. A relation is a set of ordered pairs; it may be reflexive, symmetric and transitive. An equivalence relation has all three and partitions the set into classes. A function maps each input to one output. Injective means different inputs give different outputs; surjective means every codomain value is hit; bijective means both.

sections.heading: Counting
sections.text: The sum rule adds choices for disjoint cases; the product rule multiplies independent choices. A permutation counts ordered arrangements: nPr = n! ÷ (n−r)!. A combination counts unordered selections: nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n−r)!). Example: from 5 students, choose president and secretary: 5 × 4 = 20 pairs. Choose a committee of 2: 5C2 = 5! ÷ (2!3!) = 10.

sections.heading: Graphs and number theory
sections.text: A graph has vertices and edges. A tree is a connected graph with no cycles; n vertices need n−1 edges. Graphs model networks and state machines. Number theory covers divisibility, primes, gcd and modular arithmetic. a ≡ b (mod m) means m divides a−b. Euclid’s algorithm finds gcd by repeated remainder. Example: gcd(48,18): 48 = 2×18 + 12; 18 = 1×12 + 6; 12 = 2×6 + 0, so gcd = 6. Modular arithmetic underlies hashing and cryptography.

keyPoints: Propositional logic uses truth values and connectives; predicate logic adds predicates and quantifiers ∀ and ∃.
Direct proof, contradiction and induction are standard proof techniques; induction needs a base case and an induction step.
A function maps each input to one output; injective, surjective and bijective describe how inputs and outputs match.
Counting uses the sum rule for disjoint cases and the product rule for independent choices; nPr = n! ÷ (n−r)! and nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n−r)!).
A tree is a connected graph with no cycles; n vertices need n−1 edges.
a ≡ b (mod m) means m divides a−b; Euclid’s algorithm finds gcd by repeated remainder.

en.title: Probability and statistics for engineers
en.short: Random variables, distributions, expectation, sampling, estimation, testing and regression for engineers.

sections.heading: Random variables
sections.text:
A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment. A discrete variable has a probability mass function p(x); a continuous variable has a probability density function f(x), and probabilities are areas under it. The cumulative distribution F(x)=P(X≤x) gives the probability of being at most x.

Expectation is the long-run mean: E[X]=Σ x p(x) or ∫ x f(x) dx. Variance measures spread: Var(X)=E[(X−μ)²]=E[X²]−μ², where μ=E[X]. Its square root is the standard deviation, in the same units as X.

sections.heading: Common distributions
sections.text:
The binomial counts successes in n independent trials with success probability p: mean np, variance np(1−p). The Poisson counts rare events in a fixed interval: mean and variance λ. The normal curve is set by μ and σ; standardise with z=(x−μ)/σ. The exponential models waiting times with constant failure rate λ: mean 1/λ and reliability R(t)=P(T>t)=e^(−λt).

Example: a component with mean life 1000 h and exponential life has R(500)=e^(−500/1000)=e^(−0.5)≈0.607.

sections.heading: Sampling and estimation
sections.text:
A random sample gives every item a known chance of selection. A statistic such as the sample mean x̄ estimates a population parameter. Its standard error is SE=σ/√n, often estimated by s/√n. The central limit theorem says x̄ is approximately normal for large n, whatever the population shape.

A point estimate gives one value; a confidence interval gives a range. For a normal population with known σ, a 95% interval for μ is x̄ ± 1.96σ/√n. Example: readings 10.1, 9.9, 10.0, 10.2, 9.8 V give x̄=10.0 V, s=0.158 V and SE≈0.071 V.

sections.heading: Testing and regression
sections.text:
Hypothesis testing compares data with a null hypothesis H0. The p-value is the chance of a result at least as extreme if H0 is true. Reject H0 when p is below the chosen significance level α. A Type I error rejects a true H0; a Type II error fails to reject a false H0.

Least-squares regression fits y=a+bx, with b=Sxy/Sxx and a=ȳ−b x̄, where Sxy=Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) and Sxx=Σ(x−x̄)². Correlation r measures linear strength. Plot the data: correlation is not causation.

keyPoints: Expectation is E[X]=Σ x p(x) for discrete data or ∫ x f(x) dx for continuous data, and Var(X)=E[X²]−μ².
Binomial has mean np and variance np(1−p); Poisson has mean and variance λ; standardise a normal value with z=(x−μ)/σ.
Exponential reliability is R(t)=e^(−λt) and its mean is 1/λ.
Standard error is SE=σ/√n, and the central limit theorem makes the sample mean approximately normal for large n.
A p-value below α leads to rejecting H0; Type I error rejects a true H0 and Type II error fails to reject a false H0.
Least-squares regression gives y=a+bx with b=Sxy/Sxx and a=ȳ−b x̄; correlation measures linear association only.

en.title: Circuit theory: DC networks and theorems
en.short: Covers Ohm’s and Kirchhoff’s laws, series and parallel networks, mesh and nodal analysis, Thevenin and Norton.

sections.heading: Laws and networks
sections.text:
Ohm’s law states V = IR, where V is voltage, I current and R resistance. Kirchhoff’s current law (KCL) says currents entering a node equal currents leaving it. Kirchhoff’s voltage law (KVL) says voltages around a closed loop sum to zero.

In series, current is common and resistances add: R = R1 + R2. In parallel, voltage is common and conductances add: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Two parallel resistors give R = R1R2 ÷ (R1 + R2).

sections.heading: Mesh and nodal
sections.text:
Mesh analysis writes KVL for each independent loop using mesh currents. Nodal analysis writes KCL at each independent node using node voltages, with one node as reference. Choose the method with fewer unknowns.

Example: 12 V across 4 Ω in series with a 6 Ω and 3 Ω parallel pair. The pair is 6 × 3 ÷ 9 = 2 Ω, total is 6 Ω, supply current is 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A. Parallel voltage is 2 × 2 = 4 V, so branch currents are 4 ÷ 6 = 0.667 A and 4 ÷ 3 = 1.333 A.

sections.heading: Theorems and sources
sections.text: Source transformation replaces a voltage source V in series with R by a current source I = V ÷ R in parallel with R, and the reverse. Thevenin’s theorem replaces a linear two-terminal network by VTh in series with RTh. Norton’s theorem replaces it by IN in parallel with RN, where RN = RTh and IN = VTh ÷ RTh. Superposition adds responses to each independent source alone, with other voltage sources shorted and current sources opened.

sections.heading: Maximum power
sections.text: Maximum power transfer to a load occurs when RL = RTh, giving Pmax = VTh² ÷ (4RTh). Example: VTh = 10 V, RTh = 5 Ω. With RL = 5 Ω, current is 10 ÷ 10 = 1 A and load power is 1² × 5 = 5 W. The formula gives 100 ÷ 20 = 5 W. Efficiency is 50 percent.

keyPoints: Use V = IR for a resistor; KCL balances currents at a node and KVL sums loop voltages to zero.
Series resistances add; parallel conductances add, so two parallel resistors give R1R2 ÷ (R1 + R2).
Mesh analysis uses loop currents with KVL; nodal analysis uses node voltages with KCL.
Source transformation converts V in series with R to I = V ÷ R in parallel with R, and the reverse.
Thevenin gives VTh in series with RTh; Norton gives IN = VTh ÷ RTh in parallel with RN = RTh.
Maximum load power occurs at RL = RTh and equals VTh² ÷ (4RTh); superposition applies only to linear circuits.

en.title: AC circuits, phasors and resonance
en.short: Phasors, impedance, RLC resonance, AC power and power factor, three-phase supplies and transients.

sections.heading: Sinusoids and phasors
sections.text: A sinusoid is v(t) = Vm cos(ωt + φ), where Vm is peak value, ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s and φ is phase angle. In sinusoidal steady state every voltage and current is sinusoidal at the same frequency after transients die out. A phasor is a complex number representing amplitude and phase, for example V = Vm∠φ. It removes the time factor, so derivatives become multiplication by jω. Phasor diagrams add voltages and currents as vectors.

sections.heading: Impedance and RLC
sections.text: Impedance Z = V ÷ I is the complex opposition to sinusoidal current, measured in ohms. For a resistor Z=R; for an inductor Z=jωL; for a capacitor Z=1÷(jωC)=−j÷(ωC). Admittance Y=1÷Z is measured in siemens. In series, impedances add: Z=R+j(ωL−1÷(ωC)). The current magnitude is |V|÷|Z| and its phase is shifted by the angle of Z. Example: R=10 Ω, L=20 mH, C=50 µF at f=159.15 Hz. ωL=20 Ω and 1÷(ωC)=20 Ω, so Z=10+j0 Ω. With V=100 V rms, I=10 A rms.

sections.heading: Resonance and power
sections.text: Series resonance occurs when ωL=1÷(ωC), so Z=R and current is maximum. The resonant frequency is f0=1÷(2π√(LC)). At resonance the reactances cancel, voltage and current are in phase, and power factor is 1. In general real power P=VI cosφ, reactive power Q=VI sinφ and complex power S=P+jQ, where φ is the angle between voltage and current. The magnitude |S|=VI is the apparent power. Power factor is cosφ; a low factor means more current for the same real power. In the example P=I²R=10²×10=1000 W and Q=0 var.

sections.heading: Three-phase and transients
sections.text: A balanced three-phase supply has three voltages equal in magnitude and 120° apart. In star connection the line voltage is √3 times the phase voltage, and total power is P=√3 V_L I_L cosφ. Transients are the temporary changes after switching. Capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot change instantly. In a first-order circuit they settle with time constant τ=RC or τ=L÷R; after about five time constants the change is almost complete.

keyPoints: Sinusoid: v(t)=Vm cos(ωt+φ), with ω=2πf; phasor: V=Vm∠φ.
Impedances: Z_R=R, Z_L=jωL, Z_C=1÷(jωC); series Z=R+j(ωL−1÷(ωC)).
Series resonance occurs at f0=1÷(2π√(LC)), where Z=R and current is maximum.
Real power P=VI cosφ, reactive power Q=VI sinφ and complex power S=P+jQ, with apparent power |S|=VI.
Balanced star: line voltage is √3 times phase voltage and P=√3 V_L I_L cosφ.
Capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot jump; first-order time constant is τ=RC or τ=L÷R.

en.title: Digital logic: number systems and combinational circuits
en.short: Number bases and codes, Boolean algebra, gates, Karnaugh maps, adders, multiplexers and hazards.

sections.heading: Number systems and codes
sections.text: A number system uses a base, or radix, and place values that are powers of it. Binary (base 2) uses 0 and 1; hexadecimal (base 16) uses 0 to 9 and A to F. Each hex digit stands for four bits. Example: 1011₂ = 1×8 + 0×4 + 1×2 + 1×1 = 11₁₀, and 11₁₀ = B₁₆. Codes such as BCD (binary-coded decimal) and ASCII represent decimal digits or characters as bit patterns, not as binary values.

sections.heading: Boolean algebra and gates
sections.text: Boolean algebra works with variables that take only 0 or 1. The basic operations are AND (·), OR (+) and NOT (′). Identities include A + 0 = A, A·1 = A, A + A′ = 1 and A·A′ = 0. De Morgan’s laws are (A·B)′ = A′ + B′ and (A + B)′ = A′·B′. Gates implement these operations; NAND and NOR are universal because either can build all others. A truth table lists the output for every input combination.

sections.heading: Karnaugh maps
sections.text: A Karnaugh map arranges truth-table cells so neighbours differ in one variable. Group 1s in rectangles of size 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on, using wraparound edges. Each group removes variables that change. Example: F = A′B′ + A′B + AB. The first two terms group to A′, and A′ + AB = A′ + B, so F = A′ + B. Check: when A=0, F=1; when A=1, F=B. Don’t-care cells may be grouped if they help.

sections.heading: Building blocks and hazards
sections.text: Combinational circuits have outputs that depend only on present inputs. A half adder adds two bits: sum = A⊕B, carry = A·B, where ⊕ is XOR, which outputs 1 when the two inputs differ. A full adder adds A, B and carry-in: sum = A⊕B⊕Cin, carry-out = AB + Cin(A⊕B). A comparator tests equality or order. A multiplexer selects one of several inputs using select lines. A decoder turns an n-bit code into one active output among 2ⁿ. Timing hazards are unwanted short pulses, or glitches, caused when paths have unequal delays. They can be removed with redundant terms or avoided by synchronous design.

keyPoints: Binary place values are powers of 2; each hexadecimal digit equals four bits.
De Morgan’s laws: (A·B)′ = A′ + B′ and (A + B)′ = A′·B′.
A Karnaugh map groups adjacent 1s to remove variables that change.
Half adder: sum = A⊕B, carry = A·B.
Full adder: sum = A⊕B⊕Cin, carry-out = AB + Cin(A⊕B).
Timing hazards are glitches from unequal path delays; redundant terms or synchronous design can remove them.

en.title: Programming fundamentals in C
en.short: C program structure, types, control flow, functions, arrays, pointers, structures, files and debugging.

sections.heading: Program structure
sections.text: A C program is one or more source files. Each file has declarations and function definitions, and execution starts at main. Preprocessor lines such as #include <stdio.h> bring in library declarations. Statements end with semicolons and braces group them. A variable is named storage with a type. int holds whole numbers, float and double hold real numbers, and char holds one character. Declare a variable before use; newer C standards allow declarations mixed with statements. Example: int count = 3; double price = 2.50; double total = count * price; Here total becomes 7.50.

sections.heading: Control and functions
sections.text: Control flow chooses or repeats actions: if and switch select, while and for repeat, and do while repeats at least once. Functions are named blocks that can take parameters and return a value. They reduce repetition and make testing easier. A prototype tells the compiler a function’s name, return type and parameter types before its definition. Example: int square(int x) { return x * x; } Calling square(3) returns 9.

sections.heading: Memory and data
sections.text: An array stores elements of one type in contiguous memory, indexed from 0. A pointer stores an address. The operator & gives an address and * dereferences a pointer. An array name usually converts to a pointer to its first element. A structure groups named fields of different types. Example: struct Point { int x; int y; }; struct Point p = {2, 5}; Then p.x is 2 and p.y is 5.

sections.heading: Files and debugging
sections.text: File input and output use a FILE pointer. fopen opens a file, fprintf writes and fscanf reads formatted text, and fclose closes it. Check whether fopen returns NULL. Debugging means finding and fixing defects: read compiler warnings, test small cases, add temporary printf calls, or use a debugger with breakpoints. For program design, state the problem, choose data structures, split work into functions, then test each part.

keyPoints: Every C program starts at main and uses semicolons to end statements and braces to group them.
Variables have types; int, double and char are common, and a variable must be declared before use.
if, switch, for, while and do while control which statements run and how often.
Functions can take parameters and return a value; a prototype declares a function before it is defined.
Arrays index from 0, pointers hold addresses, and structures group named fields of different types.
File input and output use fopen, fprintf or fscanf and fclose, and fopen should be checked for NULL.

en.title: Semiconductor physics and diodes
en.short: Charge carriers, the pn junction, diode models, rectifiers, special diodes and transistor basics.

sections.heading: Materials and carriers
sections.text: Silicon and germanium are semiconductors: their conductivity lies between conductors and insulators and rises with temperature. Doping adds donor atoms to make n-type material, where electrons are the majority carriers, or acceptor atoms to make p-type material, where holes are the majority carriers. A hole is a missing valence electron that behaves like a positive charge. Thermal energy creates equal numbers of electrons and holes in pure material.

sections.heading: The pn junction
sections.text: At a pn junction, electrons and holes diffuse across and leave a depletion region with fixed ionised dopants. This creates a built-in potential barrier. Forward bias, with the p side positive, lowers the barrier, so current rises roughly exponentially. Reverse bias raises it, leaving only a small reverse saturation current; excessive reverse voltage causes breakdown. The Shockley equation models the diode: I = Is(exp(V ÷ (nVT)) − 1), where VT is about 26 mV at room temperature and n is an ideality factor.

sections.heading: Diodes and rectifiers
sections.text: Diode models include the ideal switch, the constant-drop model (about 0.7 V for silicon) and the exponential model. A rectifier converts AC to DC. A half-wave rectifier uses one diode; a full-wave bridge uses four. For a sine wave of peak Vm, ideal average output is Vm ÷ π for half-wave and 2Vm ÷ π for full-wave. Example: Vm = 10 V gives 10 ÷ π = 3.18 V and 20 ÷ π = 6.37 V. A Zener diode works in reverse breakdown as a voltage reference; an LED emits light, a photodiode senses light, and a Schottky diode has a low forward drop.

sections.heading: Transistors
sections.text: A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has three regions: emitter, base and collector. In an NPN device, a small base current controls a larger collector current, so the BJT is current-controlled. A field-effect transistor (FET) has source, gate and drain; gate voltage controls channel current, so it is voltage-controlled. A MOSFET is the common insulated-gate FET used in digital circuits.

keyPoints: Doping creates n-type material with electrons as majority carriers and p-type material with holes as majority carriers.
Forward bias lowers the pn junction barrier and gives an approximately exponential current; reverse bias gives only a small saturation current until breakdown.
The Shockley diode equation is I = Is(exp(V ÷ (nVT)) − 1), with VT about 26 mV at room temperature.
The constant-drop model uses about 0.7 V for a silicon diode; Zener diodes regulate in reverse breakdown.
Ideal average rectified output is Vm ÷ π for half-wave and 2Vm ÷ π for full-wave.
A BJT is current-controlled; a MOSFET is voltage-controlled.

en.title: Sequential logic and finite state machines
en.short: Latches, flip-flops, registers, counters, synchronous design and finite state machines.

sections.heading: Latches and flip-flops
sections.text: A latch is a bistable circuit that remembers one bit. It is level-sensitive: while its enable is active, the output follows the input. A flip-flop is edge-triggered: it samples its input only at a clock edge. The D flip-flop is the workhorse; its next value is simply D. Setup time is the interval before the edge in which D must be stable, and hold time is the interval after it. Asynchronous preset and clear inputs override the clock.

sections.heading: Registers and counters
sections.text: A register is a group of flip-flops sharing one clock, so they store a word together. A shift register moves bits one position per clock. A counter is a register plus next-state logic. A ripple counter clocks each stage from the previous output; it is simple but its delay accumulates. A synchronous counter clocks all stages together, so it is faster and easier to analyse. A modulo-N counter passes through N states before repeating.

sections.heading: Synchronous design
sections.text:
Synchronous design starts with a word specification, then a state diagram and a state table. In a Moore machine the output depends only on the present state; in a Mealy machine it also depends on the input. State minimisation merges states with identical outputs and identical next states for every input. Then encode the states, derive next-state and output equations, and implement them with flip-flops and combinational logic.

Example: a modulo-4 up counter uses states 00, 01, 10, 11 and D flip-flops Q1 Q0. The sequence is 00 -> 01 -> 10 -> 11 -> 00. The next-state equations are D0 = NOT Q0 and D1 = Q1 XOR Q0. Check 01: D0 = 0, D1 = 1, giving 10.

sections.heading: FSM implementation
sections.text: Implement the FSM as next-state and output logic feeding the flip-flops. Binary encoding uses fewer flip-flops; one-hot uses one per state and often simpler logic. Simulate every state, including unused states. The clock period must exceed logic delay plus setup time.

keyPoints: A latch is level-sensitive; a flip-flop samples data at a clock edge.
A register is flip-flops with a common clock; a synchronous counter clocks all stages together.
Design flow: state diagram, state table, minimisation, encoding, next-state equations, implementation.
Moore outputs depend only on state; Mealy outputs depend on state and input.
For a modulo-4 up counter with D flip-flops, D0 = NOT Q0 and D1 = Q1 XOR Q0.
Setup and hold times must be met, and the clock period must cover logic delay plus setup time.

en.title: Computer architecture and organisation
en.short: Instruction sets, datapath and control, addressing modes, caches, I/O, buses, pipelining and performance.

sections.heading: Architecture and ISA
sections.text: Computer architecture is the programmer-visible design: the instruction set architecture (ISA). The ISA defines instructions, registers, data types, addressing modes and the memory model. Organisation is how that ISA is built: the datapath, control unit, cache sizes and bus widths. One ISA can have many organisations, so a program runs on different implementations.

sections.heading: Datapath, control and addressing
sections.text: The datapath holds the registers, arithmetic logic unit (ALU) and internal buses that carry data. The control unit decodes each instruction and sets the control signals that steer the datapath. Addressing modes say how an instruction finds its operand: immediate (value in the instruction), register, direct (memory address in the instruction), indirect (address held in memory), indexed (base plus offset) and PC-relative (offset from the program counter).

sections.heading: Memory hierarchy and caches
sections.text: The memory hierarchy places small, fast, costly memory near the CPU: registers, then cache, then main memory, then secondary storage. Caches exploit temporal locality (recent data is reused) and spatial locality (nearby data is used). A cache hit is found in cache; a miss fetches from the next level and pays a miss penalty. Average access time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.

sections.heading: I/O, buses, pipelining and performance
sections.text: Input and output can use programmed polling, interrupts or direct memory access (DMA). A bus carries addresses, data and control signals between components. Pipelining overlaps instruction stages, raising throughput, but hazards (data, control, structural) can stall it. Performance is measured by CPU time = instruction count × cycles per instruction (CPI) × clock cycle time. Example: 2.0 × 10⁹ instructions, CPI 1.5, clock 3 GHz: time = 2.0 × 10⁹ × 1.5 ÷ (3 × 10⁹) = 1.0 s.

keyPoints: ISA is the programmer-visible interface; organisation is the implementation.
CPU time = instruction count × CPI × clock cycle time.
Addressing modes include immediate, register, direct, indirect, indexed and PC-relative.
Cache average access time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.
Pipelining overlaps stages but hazards can stall it.
I/O can be programmed, interrupt-driven or DMA.

en.title: Microprocessors and microcontrollers
en.short: CPU and MCU architecture, instruction sets, addressing, interrupts, timers, serial ports and interfacing.

sections.heading: Processor and MCU
sections.text: A microprocessor is a central processing unit on one chip. It needs external memory and peripherals. A microcontroller integrates the CPU, Flash program memory, RAM, timers, serial ports and input/output pins on one chip. Both follow the fetch, decode, execute cycle. Key registers include the program counter, stack pointer, status register and general registers. Address, data and control buses connect the CPU to memory and peripherals. Memory-mapped input/output gives peripheral registers addresses in the same space as memory.

sections.heading: Instructions and addressing
sections.text: An instruction set is the CPU’s vocabulary: data movement, arithmetic, logic, branches, calls and input/output. Reduced instruction set (RISC) designs favour simple fixed-length instructions; complex instruction set (CISC) designs offer richer instructions. Addressing modes state where an operand is: immediate (in the instruction), register, direct, indirect, indexed or relative. For example, load R1, [R2+4] uses indexed addressing: the address is R2 plus 4. The programmer or compiler chooses modes to save instructions and time.

sections.heading: Interrupts, timers, serial
sections.text: An interrupt suspends the main program, runs an interrupt service routine (ISR), then returns. The vector table gives each interrupt its start address; priority and masking control nesting. A timer counts clock ticks. A prescaler divides the input clock. Serial ports such as UART send bits one after another at an agreed baud rate, with start and stop framing. Example: a 16 MHz timer clock with prescaler 64 ticks every 64 ÷ 16,000,000 = 4 µs. For a 1 ms delay, count 0.001 ÷ 0.000004 = 250 ticks.

sections.heading: Interfacing and programming
sections.text: Peripherals connect through general-purpose input/output pins, serial buses such as I2C and SPI, or memory-mapped registers. Device programming means writing configuration values to those registers and servicing flags. Use volatile pointers for registers that hardware changes, read the datasheet, set pin directions, enable clocks, and handle interrupts. Check voltage levels and current limits before connecting a device.

keyPoints: A microcontroller integrates CPU, memory, timers, serial ports and I/O; a microprocessor is mainly the CPU.
Addressing modes include immediate, register, direct, indirect, indexed and relative.
Interrupts use a vector table and ISR; priority and masking manage nesting.
Timer tick = prescaler ÷ clock frequency, and counts = delay ÷ tick.
UART communication needs matching baud rate and framing at both ends.
Program peripherals through memory-mapped registers; use volatile and read the datasheet.

en.title: Assembly language and low-level programming
en.short: Assembly syntax, calling conventions, stack frames, C interoperation, startup code and device drivers.

sections.heading: Assembly basics
sections.text: Assembly language is a human-readable form of a processor’s machine instructions. A line usually holds one instruction, such as mov, add, load or branch, with operands naming registers, memory or constants. Registers are small storage inside the CPU. Memory is addressed by number. An assembler translates the text to machine code; a linker combines the object files and assigns addresses. Assembly is processor-specific: ARM, RISC-V and x86 have different instructions, so code is not portable.

sections.heading: Calls and stack frames
sections.text: A calling convention is an agreement on how arguments are passed, how a value is returned, and which registers the callee (called function) must preserve. The stack is memory that grows and shrinks with calls. A stack frame holds saved registers, local variables and the return address. On 32-bit x86 with the cdecl convention, the caller pushes arguments right to left, call pushes the return address, and the callee saves ebp, sets ebp = esp and subtracts space for locals. Thus [ebp+8] is the first argument. Other ABIs (application binary interfaces) differ, so check the ABI.

sections.heading: Mixing with C
sections.text: C code can call assembly routines and assembly can call C functions if both follow the same ABI. Compilers offer inline assembly, which inserts instructions into a C function, and separate assembly files linked with C. Declare the interface exactly, keep the stack balanced, and list registers changed. A common case is a short time-critical loop or a special instruction that C cannot express.

sections.heading: Startup and drivers
sections.text: Startup code runs before main. It sets the stack pointer, clears or initialises memory, copies initialised data, and calls main. A linker script decides where code and data are placed. A device driver talks to hardware through registers. With memory-mapped I/O, device registers appear at fixed addresses; the driver reads and writes them, often using volatile pointers so the compiler does not remove the accesses. Interrupt handlers need care: save state and return correctly. Details depend on the processor and board.

keyPoints: Assembly is processor-specific and maps closely to machine instructions.
A calling convention fixes argument passing, return values and register preservation; ABIs differ by platform.
A stack frame holds the return address, saved registers and locals; keep the stack balanced.
Mixing C and assembly requires matching the ABI and declaring the interface exactly.
Startup code prepares the machine and calls main; linker scripts place code and data.
Device drivers access hardware registers, often through volatile memory-mapped I/O.

en.title: Analogue electronic circuits
en.short: Biasing, small-signal models, amplifiers, frequency response, feedback and power classes.

sections.heading: Biasing
sections.text:
Biasing sets a transistor’s DC operating point (Q point) so it stays in the active region for the whole signal swing. In BJT voltage-divider bias, R1 and R2 set the base voltage, RE stabilises emitter current, and RC sets collector voltage. A FET needs a gate-source voltage; self-bias uses a source resistor. The Q point must leave room for the swing, or the signal clips.

Example: VCC = 12 V, R1 = 47 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, RE = 1 kΩ, RC = 2.2 kΩ, β large.
VB = 12 × 10 ÷ 57 = 2.105 V
VE = 2.105 − 0.7 = 1.405 V
IE = 1.405 ÷ 1 kΩ = 1.405 mA
VC = 12 − 1.405 × 2.2 = 8.909 V
VCE = 8.909 − 1.405 = 7.504 V

sections.heading: Small-signal amplifiers
sections.text: Once biased, replace the transistor by a small-signal model. The BJT hybrid-pi model uses transconductance gm = IC ÷ VT, where VT is the thermal voltage (about 26 mV at room temperature), input resistance rπ = β ÷ gm, and output resistance ro. The FET model uses gm and ro. A single stage is common-emitter/source (voltage gain, inverted), common-base/gate (voltage gain, low input resistance), or common-collector/drain (voltage buffer). Multistage gain is the product of stage gains, but loading reduces it.

sections.heading: Frequency and feedback
sections.text:
Frequency response is limited at low frequency by coupling and bypass capacitors and at high frequency by transistor capacitances. The Miller effect multiplies the input-to-output capacitance, lowering the high cutoff. Gain falls by 3 dB at each cutoff; the gain-bandwidth product is roughly constant.

Negative feedback takes a fraction β of the output back to the input. It reduces gain by a factor of 1 + βA, widens bandwidth, lowers distortion, and changes input and output resistance depending on topology. Stability must be checked.

sections.heading: Power amplifiers
sections.text: Power amplifiers are classed by conduction angle. Class A conducts all the time, has low distortion and low ideal efficiency (25% with a resistive load). Class B push-pull conducts half the cycle and has ideal efficiency 78.5% but crossover distortion. Class AB reduces that distortion. Class C is efficient but very distorted, used in tuned radio. Class D switches and is very efficient.

keyPoints: Biasing sets the Q point; voltage-divider bias uses VB = VCC R2 ÷ (R1 + R2) and VE = VB − VBE.
Small-signal BJT parameters: gm = IC ÷ VT and rπ = β ÷ gm.
Single-stage gain depends on transconductance and load; multistage gain is the product of stage gains after loading.
Low cutoff comes from coupling and bypass capacitors; high cutoff comes from transistor capacitances and the Miller effect.
Negative feedback reduces gain by a factor of 1 + βA and can widen bandwidth and lower distortion.
Class A ideal efficiency is 25% with a resistive load, class B 78.5%; class AB and class D trade distortion and efficiency.

en.title: Operational amplifiers and signal conditioning
en.short: Ideal and practical op-amps, amplifier configurations, active filters, instrumentation amps and sensor conditioning.

sections.heading: Op-amp behaviour
sections.text:
An operational amplifier (op-amp) is a high-gain differential voltage amplifier. The ideal model has infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance, zero output impedance and zero input current. With negative feedback, the summing-point idea gives V+ ≈ V−, so the external components set the gain.

Real op-amps depart from this: finite gain and bandwidth, input offset voltage, bias currents, finite output swing and slew rate (the maximum rate of output change). These limits matter for small sensor signals, high gain and fast edges.

sections.heading: Basic configurations
sections.text:
The inverting amplifier gives Vout = −(Rf ÷ Rin) Vin and presents a virtual earth (a node held near 0 V without a direct ground connection) at its input. The non-inverting amplifier gives Vout = (1 + Rf ÷ Rin) Vin and has high input impedance. Both need negative feedback and a defined input path.

Example: inverting amplifier with Rin = 10 kΩ, Rf = 100 kΩ and Vin = 50 mV. Gain = −100 ÷ 10 = −10, so Vout = −10 × 50 mV = −0.5 V.

sections.heading: Filters and instrumentation
sections.text:
Active filters use resistors, capacitors and an op-amp to shape frequency response; they can add gain and avoid loading. A first-order RC low-pass has cutoff fc = 1 ÷ (2πRC). Sallen-Key is a common second-order topology.

An instrumentation amplifier is a difference amplifier with very high input impedance and gain set by one resistor. It amplifies the small difference between sensor outputs while rejecting common-mode noise, measured by common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR).

sections.heading: Comparators, oscillators and sensors
sections.text:
A comparator compares two voltages and drives its output to a supply rail; open-loop use is fast but noisy, so hysteresis (two slightly different switching thresholds) is often added. An oscillator uses positive feedback and a frequency-selective network; a Wien bridge with equal R and C oscillates near f = 1 ÷ (2πRC).

Sensor conditioning prepares a sensor signal for conversion: buffering, amplification, filtering, offset removal and bridge excitation (supply voltage for a sensor bridge). Check the op-amp’s input range, output swing and stability.

keyPoints: With negative feedback, an ideal op-amp keeps V+ ≈ V− and draws no input current.
Inverting gain is −Rf ÷ Rin; non-inverting gain is 1 + Rf ÷ Rin.
Real op-amps have finite gain, bandwidth, output swing and slew rate, plus offset and bias currents.
A first-order RC active low-pass filter has cutoff fc = 1 ÷ (2πRC).
An instrumentation amplifier has high input impedance and high common-mode rejection, with gain set by one resistor.
Comparators usually need hysteresis, and a Wien bridge oscillator with equal R and C runs near f = 1 ÷ (2πRC).

en.title: Signals and systems: continuous and discrete
en.short: Continuous and discrete signals, convolution, Fourier, Laplace and z transforms, sampling and system properties.

sections.heading: Signals
sections.text: A signal carries information as a function of time. A continuous-time signal x(t) is defined at every instant; a discrete-time signal x[n] only at integer n. The unit impulse δ[n] is 1 at n = 0 and 0 elsewhere. The unit step u[n] is 0 for n < 0 and 1 for n ≥ 0. Periodic signals repeat after a period T or N samples.

sections.heading: Convolution and LTI
sections.text: An LTI system is linear and time-invariant. Linearity means superposition: input a x1 + b x2 gives output a y1 + b y2. Time invariance means a delayed input gives the same delayed output. An LTI system is fully described by its impulse response h. Its output is convolution: y(t) = integral x(τ)h(t − τ)dτ, or y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k]. Example: x[n] = [1, 2, 1] and h[n] = [1, 1] give y[n] = [1, 3, 3, 1]. Check: y[1] = 1×1 + 2×1 = 3.

sections.heading: Transforms
sections.text: The Fourier series writes a periodic signal as a sum of sines and cosines at harmonics. The Fourier transform X(ω) = integral x(t)e^(−jωt)dt gives the frequency content of an aperiodic signal. The Laplace transform generalises it with complex s, and its region of convergence (ROC) must be stated. For discrete signals the z transform X(z) = Σ x[n]z^(−n) plays the same role. Poles and ROCs reveal stability and causality.

sections.heading: Sampling and properties
sections.text: Sampling converts x(t) to x[n] = x(nT), where T is the sampling interval. The sampling theorem says the rate must exceed twice the highest frequency, or aliasing folds high frequencies onto low ones. System properties: causal output depends only on present and past inputs; stable means every bounded input gives a bounded output (BIBO). For an LTI system, BIBO stability requires the impulse response to be absolutely summable, Σ|h[n]| finite, or absolutely integrable in continuous time.

keyPoints: Convolution for an LTI system is y(t) = integral x(τ)h(t − τ)dτ and y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k].
Linearity means superposition, and time invariance means a delayed input gives the same delayed output.
Fourier series represent periodic signals; Fourier transforms represent aperiodic signals in frequency.
Laplace and z transforms use complex variables and require a region of convergence.
The sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency to avoid aliasing.
An LTI system is causal if h(t) = 0 for t < 0 or h[n] = 0 for n < 0, and BIBO stable if Σ|h[n]| or integral |h(t)|dt is finite.

en.title: Digital signal processing
en.short: Discrete-time systems, DFT and FFT, FIR and IIR filter design, windowing, quantisation and processor implementation.

sections.heading: Discrete-time systems
sections.text: A discrete-time signal x[n] is a sequence of samples, usually taken at a fixed rate fs. A linear time-invariant (LTI) system is described by its impulse response h[n] or by a difference equation such as y[n] = 0.5y[n−1] + x[n]. The output is the convolution y[n] = Σ h[k]x[n−k]. The z-transform turns convolution into multiplication, and the system is stable when every pole lies inside the unit circle. For that example the pole is at z = 0.5, so the system is stable; a unit step input gives y[0] = 1, y[1] = 1.5, y[2] = 1.75, settling towards 2.

sections.heading: DFT and FFT
sections.text: The N-point discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is X[k] = Σ x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N), for k = 0 to N−1. It samples the spectrum at frequencies k fs/N. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes the same values in O(N log N) operations instead of O(N²). Example: x = [1, 0, 1, 0] with N = 4 gives X = [2, 0, 2, 0], because the even samples add at k = 0 and k = 2 and cancel at k = 1 and k = 3.

sections.heading: FIR and IIR filters
sections.text: A finite impulse response (FIR) filter has h[n] = 0 beyond a fixed length. It is always stable and can have exactly linear phase. An infinite impulse response (IIR) filter uses feedback, so it can be unstable and has nonlinear phase, but it needs a lower order for a sharp cutoff. Window methods design FIR filters by multiplying the ideal impulse response by a window such as rectangular or Hamming; this reduces ripple but widens the transition band. IIR filters are often designed by the bilinear transform.

sections.heading: Quantisation and implementation
sections.text: Quantisation rounds signal samples and filter coefficients to a fixed number of bits. It adds noise, can cause limit cycles in IIR filters, and changes the frequency response. Fixed-point DSP processors use multiply-accumulate (MAC) units and circular buffers to run convolution and filtering in real time. Floating-point processors reduce quantisation error but usually cost more and use more power.

keyPoints: A discrete-time LTI system is described by its impulse response or a difference equation; convolution gives the output.
The N-point DFT is X[k] = Σ x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N), with frequency spacing fs/N.
The FFT computes the DFT in O(N log N) operations instead of O(N²).
FIR filters are always stable and can be linear phase; IIR filters use feedback and may be unstable.
Windowing shapes an FIR impulse response but trades ripple against transition width.
Quantisation adds noise and can cause limit cycles; fixed-point DSPs use MAC units.

en.title: Control systems
en.short: Transfer functions, state equations, block diagrams, stability tests, root locus, Bode, Nyquist, errors and PID.

sections.heading: Modelling and block diagrams
sections.text:
A control system is modelled by a transfer function G(s) = Y(s) ÷ U(s), the Laplace ratio with zero initial conditions, or by state equations x' = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du. Poles are roots of the denominator and shape the natural response.

Block diagram reduction uses series multiplication, parallel addition, and negative feedback G ÷ (1 + GH). The characteristic equation 1 + GH = 0 gives closed-loop poles.

sections.heading: Routh-Hurwitz stability
sections.text:
A linear system is stable when every pole has a negative real part. Routh-Hurwitz builds a table from the characteristic polynomial. The number of sign changes in the first column equals the number of right-half-plane poles.

Example: s³ + s² + 2s + 8.
s³: 1, 2
s²: 1, 8
s¹: (1×2 − 1×8) ÷ 1 = −6
s⁰: 8
First column 1, 1, −6, 8 has two sign changes, so two poles lie in the right half-plane and the system is unstable.

sections.heading: Root locus and frequency
sections.text: The root locus shows closed-loop poles as a gain K varies. Branches start at open-loop poles and end at open-loop zeros or infinity. Bode plots show magnitude and phase against frequency; gain margin and phase margin measure how far the loop is from instability. The Nyquist plot traces G(jω) in the complex plane, and encirclements of −1 decide closed-loop stability.

sections.heading: Steady-state error and PID
sections.text:
For unity feedback, position, velocity and acceleration constants are Kp = lim s→0 G(s), Kv = lim s→0 sG(s), Ka = lim s→0 s²G(s). Step, ramp and parabolic errors are 1 ÷ (1 + Kp), 1 ÷ Kv and 1 ÷ Ka.

PID control uses u = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt + Kd de/dt. Kp speeds response, Ki removes offset, Kd damps.

Example: G = 10 ÷ [s(s + 2)]. Kv = lim s→0 sG = 10 ÷ 2 = 5, so a ramp gives ess = 1 ÷ 5 = 0.2.

keyPoints: Transfer function: G(s) = Y(s) ÷ U(s); state form: x' = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du.
Negative feedback reduces to G ÷ (1 + GH); closed-loop poles solve 1 + GH = 0.
Routh-Hurwitz: sign changes in the first column equal right-half-plane poles.
Root locus branches start at open-loop poles and end at open-loop zeros or infinity as gain varies.
Bode and Nyquist methods use gain margin, phase margin and encirclements of −1 to judge stability.
For unity feedback, ess = 1 ÷ (1 + Kp) for step, 1 ÷ Kv for ramp, 1 ÷ Ka for parabola; PID is u = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt + Kd de/dt.

en.title: Data communications and networking
en.short: Signals, modulation, media, error control, OSI and TCP/IP layering, IP addressing, routing and LANs.

sections.heading: Signals and media
sections.text: Data is carried as a signal: a time-varying voltage, current, light or radio wave. A channel is the path and band of frequencies it occupies. Bandwidth is the range of frequencies, while data rate is bits per second. Baseband sends digital pulses directly; passband shifts them onto a carrier. Media are guided (twisted pair, coaxial cable, optical fibre) or unguided (radio, microwave). Fibre has high bandwidth and immunity to electrical noise; copper is cheap and easy to terminate.

sections.heading: Modulation and errors
sections.text: Modulation maps bits onto carrier properties: amplitude (ASK), frequency (FSK), phase (PSK) or a mix (QAM). Higher-order QAM carries more bits per symbol but needs a better signal-to-noise ratio. Errors are detected with parity, checksums and CRC, and corrected by forward error correction or by retransmission (ARQ). CRC is strong for burst errors; parity is weak.

sections.heading: Layering and IP
sections.text: Layering divides the task. The OSI reference model has seven layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application. TCP/IP uses four: link, internet, transport, application. Each layer adds a header, a process called encapsulation. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits; IPv6 are 128 bits. A prefix length gives the network part. Example: a /26 has mask 255.255.255.192 and block size 64, so 192.168.10.0/24 splits into subnets .0, .64, .128 and .192, with 62 usable hosts each.

sections.heading: Routing and LANs
sections.text: Routing selects paths between networks. A router forwards packets by longest-prefix match on a routing table. Interior protocols include OSPF; BGP carries routes between autonomous systems. A LAN connects devices in a limited area. Ethernet is the dominant wired LAN standard; Wi-Fi is common wireless. Switches forward frames by MAC address within a LAN, while routers move packets between LANs.

keyPoints: Nyquist gives the maximum bit rate for a noiseless channel: C = 2B log2 M bits per second, where M is the number of signal levels.
Shannon gives capacity for a noisy channel: C = B log2(1 + S/N).
OSI has seven layers; TCP/IP has four, and encapsulation adds headers at each layer.
A /26 IPv4 subnet has 64 addresses and 62 usable hosts.
CRC detects burst errors better than simple parity.
Routers forward by longest-prefix match; switches forward frames by MAC address.

en.title: Embedded systems design
en.short: Specification, processor choice, sensor and bus interfacing, real-time timing, power and reliability.

sections.heading: Specification and processor choice
sections.text:
A specification states what the embedded system must do and the limits it must meet: functions, interfaces, speed, memory, power, environment, cost and tests.

Processor selection follows the specification. Compare throughput, memory, on-chip peripherals, power modes, temperature range, cost, toolchain and long-term supply. A microcontroller suits control and low power; a microprocessor or system-on-chip suits heavier computing. Choose the smallest part that meets worst-case load with margin.

sections.heading: Interfacing and buses
sections.text:
Sensors convert physical quantities into electrical signals. Condition the signal (amplify, filter, protect), then digitise with an ADC or read a digital output. Actuators need drivers and protection against inductive kickback.

UART is an asynchronous point-to-point link with an agreed baud rate and frame format. SPI is a synchronous master-slave bus with clock, data and chip-select lines; it is fast but uses more pins. I2C is a two-wire addressed bus that shares many devices, but it is slower and needs pull-up resistors. Choose by speed, distance, pin count and device count.

sections.heading: Real-time and power
sections.text:
A real-time system must finish work by a deadline. Hard deadlines can cause failure; soft deadlines only reduce quality. Analyse worst-case execution time, interrupt latency and jitter. Use priorities, timers and a real-time operating system where needed.

Power comes from duty cycling. Example: a node draws 12 mA for 20 ms each second and 5 uA otherwise. Active duty = 0.02 s ÷ 1 s = 2%. Average current = 12 mA × 0.02 + 0.005 mA × 0.98 = 0.24 + 0.0049 = 0.2449 mA. A 1000 mAh battery gives about 1000 ÷ 0.2449 = 4083 h, or 170 days, ignoring losses.

sections.heading: Reliability
sections.text: Reliability means the system keeps working, or fails safely, over its life. Use a watchdog timer, brown-out detection, memory checks and input protection. Test at temperature and supply extremes, and check electromagnetic compatibility. Safety and EMC rules vary by country and product type; confirm local requirements. Professional registration differs by country, for example COREN in Nigeria.

keyPoints: A specification fixes functions, interfaces, limits and tests before design starts.
Choose the smallest processor that meets worst-case load, memory, power and environment needs.
UART is asynchronous point-to-point; SPI is fast synchronous master-slave; I2C is a slower two-wire addressed bus.
Hard real-time tasks must meet every deadline; analyse worst-case execution time, latency and jitter.
Average current = sum of (current × duty fraction); battery life ≈ capacity ÷ average current.
Use watchdog, brown-out detection, memory checks and protection, and check local safety and EMC rules.

en.title: Digital system design with HDL and FPGAs
en.short: HDL, simulation, synthesis, synchronous design, testbenches, timing closure and FPGA implementation.

sections.heading: HDL and simulation
sections.text: A hardware description language (HDL) is a text language for describing digital hardware. Verilog and VHDL are the two common ones. You write modules with inputs, outputs and internal signals. Simulation runs the code on a computer with a testbench, which applies stimulus and checks outputs. A testbench is not synthesised; it may use delays and file input. Simulation answers whether the design behaves as intended before hardware exists.

sections.heading: Synthesis and FPGAs
sections.text: Synthesis translates the synthesisable subset of HDL into gates or lookup tables. Not every HDL statement can be synthesised: delays and file operations are simulation only. On a field-programmable gate array (FPGA), logic is built from lookup tables, flip-flops, block memory and routing. The implementation flow is synthesis, place and route, static timing analysis, then bitstream generation. Tools differ by vendor, so check the tool documentation.

sections.heading: Synchronous practice
sections.text: Synchronous design uses a clock to control flip-flops. Keep one clock per design where possible, use clock enables rather than gated clocks, and use a single asynchronous reset strategy. Register inputs and outputs at module boundaries. Signals that cross clock domains need synchronisers, such as two flip-flops in series for a single-bit signal. Avoid combinational feedback and latches created by incomplete if or case statements.

sections.heading: Timing closure
sections.text: Timing closure means the design meets setup and hold checks at the chosen clock rate. Static timing analysis reports slack: positive slack passes, negative slack fails. A simplified setup check is slack = Tclk − (Tco + Tcomb + Tsetup), ignoring skew and jitter. Here Tco is the clock-to-output delay of the launching flip-flop, Tcomb is the delay of the combinational logic between the flip-flops, and Tsetup is the setup time of the capturing flip-flop. Example: Tclk = 10 ns, Tco = 1.5 ns, Tcomb = 6.0 ns, Tsetup = 0.5 ns. Slack = 10 − (1.5 + 6.0 + 0.5) = 2.0 ns, so the path passes. Fix negative slack by pipelining, reducing logic depth or changing the clock constraint.

keyPoints: An HDL describes hardware; simulation checks behaviour and synthesis maps synthesisable code to gates or lookup tables.
A testbench applies stimulus and checks outputs, and it is not synthesised into hardware.
Synchronous design uses one clock where possible, clock enables, and synchronisers for clock-domain crossings.
Setup slack is Tclk − (Tco + Tcomb + Tsetup) when skew and jitter are ignored.
Positive slack meets the timing check; negative slack requires pipelining, less logic depth or a different constraint.
On an FPGA the flow is synthesis, place and route, timing analysis and bitstream generation.

en.title: VLSI design fundamentals
en.short: MOS behaviour, CMOS logic and layout, design rules, logic families, delay, power and the ASIC flow.

sections.heading: MOS transistor
sections.text: An MOS transistor is a voltage-controlled switch. An NMOS device conducts when gate-source voltage exceeds threshold voltage Vt; a PMOS device conducts when its gate-source voltage is below its threshold voltage Vt, which is negative for PMOS. The insulated gate draws almost no steady current, but charging channel and parasitic capacitance causes delay and dynamic power. Digital design models it as a switch with on-resistance and capacitance.

sections.heading: CMOS logic and layout
sections.text:
Static CMOS gates pair a pull-up network of PMOS transistors with a pull-down network of NMOS transistors. For every valid input one network conducts, so the output is always driven and no static path runs from supply to ground.

Layout places transistors in diffusion, polysilicon gates cross it, and metal connects them. Design rules are the foundry’s minimum widths, spacings and enclosures that keep the process manufacturable; they change with each technology node. DRC checks the rules; LVS checks layout against schematic.

sections.heading: Logic families and timing
sections.text:
Static CMOS is the default family. Dynamic logic precharges a node, then evaluates through NMOS devices. It can be faster but suffers charge leakage and charge sharing, and needs clock power.

Propagation delay is roughly t_pd ≈ 0.69 R_eq C_load. Dynamic power is P = α C V² f, where α is switching activity, C switched capacitance, V supply and f frequency. Leakage adds static power.

Example: α = 0.1, C = 20 pF, V = 1.8 V, f = 200 MHz.
P = 0.1 × 20×10⁻¹² × 1.8² × 200×10⁶ = 1.296 mW.

sections.heading: ASIC flow
sections.text: The ASIC design flow starts from a specification and register-transfer-level (RTL) code. Simulation checks function. Synthesis maps RTL to a gate netlist using a standard-cell library. Floorplanning, placement and clock-tree synthesis arrange cells; routing connects them. Static timing analysis, power analysis, DRC and LVS sign off the layout before tapeout and fabrication. Fabricated chips are then tested.

keyPoints: An NMOS transistor conducts when its gate-source voltage is above Vt; a PMOS transistor conducts when its gate-source voltage is below Vt, which is negative for PMOS.
Static CMOS uses complementary pull-up PMOS and pull-down NMOS networks, so valid inputs always drive the output.
Design rules are foundry-specific minimum geometry and spacing rules checked by DRC; LVS compares layout with schematic.
Dynamic logic precharges and evaluates on clock phases, but risks charge leakage and charge sharing.
For a simple RC load, propagation delay is roughly t_pd ≈ 0.69 R_eq C_load.
Dynamic power is P = α C V² f, where α is switching activity, C is switched capacitance, V is supply voltage and f is frequency.

en.title: Real-time operating systems
en.short: Tasks, scheduling, priority inversion, interrupts, memory and meeting deadlines in embedded RTOS.

sections.heading: Tasks and scheduling
sections.text:
A real-time operating system (RTOS) runs several tasks, each with its own stack and state: ready, running, blocked or suspended. A preemptive priority scheduler switches tasks on events or timer ticks. A hard deadline must never be missed; a soft deadline may occasionally slip.

Rate monotonic scheduling gives shorter periods higher priority. For n independent periodic tasks with deadlines equal to periods, the sufficient utilisation bound is U ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1), where U = Σ(Ci ÷ Ti), Ci is worst-case execution time and Ti is period. For two tasks the bound is 0.828. Example: C1 = 2 ms, T1 = 10 ms; C2 = 4 ms, T2 = 20 ms. U = 2/10 + 4/20 = 0.4, it passes. Earliest deadline first can use U ≤ 1 with implicit deadlines.

sections.heading: Sharing and blocking
sections.text:
Tasks share data through semaphores, mutexes and message queues. A counting semaphore guards a pool of resources; a mutex gives exclusive access. A queue passes data between tasks without shared variables.

Priority inversion happens when a high-priority task waits for a mutex held by a low-priority task, and a medium-priority task preempts the low one. The high task waits far longer than expected. Priority inheritance makes the low task inherit the high priority while it holds the lock. Watch for deadlock and unbounded blocking.

sections.heading: Interrupts and memory
sections.text:
An interrupt service routine (ISR) should be short. It acknowledges the device, saves minimal state and defers work to a task. Interrupt latency is the time from the interrupt request to the first instruction of the ISR; it affects deadlines.

Embedded RTOSs usually avoid virtual memory because address translation and page faults make timing unpredictable. Memory is allocated statically or from fixed-size pools. Each task has a stack, and stack overflow is a common failure. Check high-water marks.

sections.heading: Meeting deadlines
sections.text: Meeting deadlines needs worst-case execution time (WCET) estimates, response-time analysis and measurement. Jitter, the variation in response time, matters in control loops. Test overload and interrupt storms.

keyPoints: An RTOS schedules tasks by priority, preempting on events or timer ticks; hard deadlines must never be missed.
Rate monotonic utilisation bound: U = Σ(Ci ÷ Ti) ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1); for two tasks the bound is about 0.828.
Priority inversion occurs when a medium-priority task delays a high-priority task waiting on a low-priority lock holder; priority inheritance limits it.
Keep interrupt service routines short and defer work to tasks to control interrupt latency.
Embedded RTOS memory is usually static or pool-based; avoid virtual memory and check for stack overflow.
Meeting deadlines needs WCET estimates, response-time analysis and measurement, and jitter matters in control loops.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and registration
en.short: Regulation, ethics, standards, liability, safety, sustainability and registration, with country examples.

sections.heading: Profession and regulation
sections.text:
Engineering is a profession: it applies specialised knowledge, serves public safety and accepts self-regulation. Regulation protects the public: laws may reserve titles and require registration for certain work.

In Nigeria, COREN (Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria) is the statutory regulator. In the UK, the Engineering Council keeps the register and licensed institutions such as the IET assess candidates. In the US, state boards license professional engineers; IEEE is a professional association, not a licence issuer. Rules differ, so check your country’s current official requirements.

sections.heading: Ethics and liability
sections.text:
Codes of ethics state duties: competence, honesty, public safety first, confidentiality and conflict avoidance. IEEE and IET publish such codes. A code is not a statute, but breach can lead to discipline and may be evidence in court. Liability can arise in contract, negligence or product liability. Professional indemnity insurance covers claims.

Case: Ada, an engineer in Lagos, refuses to sign off a mains power board because conductor spacing is too small for the stated voltage. She records the finding and asks for a redesign. Signing would misrepresent safety and expose her employer to liability.

sections.heading: Standards and safety
sections.text:
Standards are agreed technical rules; codes of practice give guidance. They become mandatory when a law or contract says so. Health and safety uses hazard and risk assessment: identify hazards, estimate risk and control them.

Design out hazards where possible, use fail-safe behaviour and warn users. Sustainability considers energy use, materials, repairability and electronic waste over the product lifecycle. In computer engineering, safety also covers mains isolation, battery protection, electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) and software that fails safely.

sections.heading: Registration and CPD
sections.text:
Registration usually requires an accredited degree, supervised experience, a professional review and continuing professional development (CPD). CPD keeps knowledge and skills current.

Disciplinary panels can suspend or remove registration. Requirements vary by country and change over time, so check the current rules of COREN, the Engineering Council and IET, or your local state board before you apply.

keyPoints: Engineering regulation protects the public by reserving titles and requiring registration for certain work.
COREN is Nigeria’s statutory engineering regulator; the UK Engineering Council and IET, and US state boards, have different roles.
Codes of ethics require competence, honesty, public safety first and disclosure of conflicts.
Standards become mandatory only when a law or contract makes them so.
Liability can arise from contract, negligence or product liability, and professional indemnity insurance covers claims.
Registration needs accredited education, supervised experience, professional review and CPD; check current national rules.

en.title: Computer engineering design project
en.short: Problem definition, specification, design, prototyping, testing, documentation and presentation.

sections.heading: Problem definition
sections.text:
A capstone starts with a real need, not a solution. Write a problem statement that names the user, the setting and the pain. Example: Amina’s team at a Nigerian polytechnic helps small vegetable farms that lose seedlings to dry soil. State who needs what, and list constraints: cost, power and local spares.

Turn the statement into a specification: measurable requirements, interfaces, operating conditions and acceptance criteria. Separate must-have from nice-to-have. A requirement such as “the unit must run for seven days on one charge” can be tested; “it must be reliable” cannot.

sections.heading: Review and standards
sections.text:
Review literature, datasheets, prior projects and standards. Standards are not universal: electrical safety, radio emissions and environmental rules differ by country. In Nigeria, professional engineering registration is through COREN; other countries have their own bodies. Check the current official source; do not copy clause numbers or limits.

Record what you read and why it changes your design. A short review table with source, finding and decision is enough. It shows that your choices rest on evidence, not guesswork.

sections.heading: Design and prototype
sections.text:
Use a structured method: block diagram, interfaces, trade-off table, detailed design. Hold design reviews at each stage. Keep requirements, diagrams and code under version control. Prototype early: breadboard, development board, PCB, enclosure. Test each block before joining them.

For the farm unit, the team compares a mains-powered node with a solar-powered one. Solar wins on installation cost but needs battery sizing and sleep modes. The trade-off table records the reason.

sections.heading: Testing and presentation
sections.text:
Test against the specification, not hope. Use unit, integration and field tests. Record each result, including failures. Acceptance testing asks whether the user can do the task reliably.

Document requirements, design, test log, user manual and known limits. Present with a live demo, clear slides and a short viva. State what works, what does not, and what you would do next. Honest limits earn more credit than hidden faults.

keyPoints: Start from a real user need and write a problem statement before choosing a solution.
A good specification has measurable requirements, defined interfaces and acceptance criteria.
Standards and professional registration differ by country; in Nigeria registration is through COREN, so check the current official source.
Use design reviews, trade-off tables and version control to keep design decisions traceable.
Prototype in stages and test each block, then the whole system, against the specification.
Document requirements, design, tests and limits, and present honestly what works and what does not.

en.title: Advanced computer architecture: pipelines, parallelism and accelerators
en.short: Pipelining, ILP, superscalar, out-of-order, prediction, multicore, cache coherence and accelerators.

sections.heading: Pipelining and hazards
sections.text: Pipelining overlaps instruction stages, so throughput rises even though each instruction still takes the same latency. Speedup is limited by the slowest stage and by hazards. A structural hazard means two instructions need one resource. A data hazard means an instruction needs a result not yet written; forwarding can supply it, otherwise the pipeline stalls. A control hazard follows a branch whose outcome is unknown. Ideal case: five stages, one cycle each, 100 instructions. Non-pipelined time = 100 × 5 = 500 cycles. Pipelined time = 5 + (100 − 1) = 104 cycles, so speedup = 500 ÷ 104 ≈ 4.81. Real speedup is lower because of hazards.

sections.heading: ILP and prediction
sections.text: Instruction-level parallelism (ILP) overlaps independent instructions. Superscalar processors issue several instructions per cycle; out-of-order execution issues them when operands are ready and retires them in program order using a reorder buffer. Register renaming removes false dependencies. Branch prediction guesses a branch outcome; a misprediction flushes the pipeline and costs cycles. Static predictors use fixed rules or opcode; dynamic predictors use branch history tables. Accuracy matters.

sections.heading: Multicore and coherence
sections.text: A multicore processor puts several cores on one chip. Shared memory needs cache coherence: all cores must see writes to one address in a consistent order. Snooping and directory protocols are common. False sharing occurs when unrelated variables share a cache line and cores contend. Memory consistency defines the order of loads and stores across cores; sequential consistency is the strict model, while weaker models allow reordering and need fences. These rules are architectural, not tied to one country.

sections.heading: Accelerators
sections.text: Accelerators are specialised units, such as GPUs, FPGAs or AI accelerators, that offload regular parallel work from the CPU. They trade generality for throughput and energy efficiency. The CPU still manages data movement, which can dominate. A simple case: a data-parallel matrix task suits a GPU; a small control-heavy task may run faster on the CPU. Design choices depend on workload, memory bandwidth and programming model.

keyPoints: Pipeline ideal time for k stages and n instructions is k + n − 1 cycles; speedup is non-pipelined time divided by this.
Hazards are structural, data or control; forwarding and stalls manage data hazards.
Superscalar and out-of-order execution raise ILP but must retire instructions in program order.
Branch mispredictions flush the pipeline, so prediction accuracy affects performance.
Cache coherence keeps shared data consistent; memory consistency defines load/store ordering across cores.
Accelerators improve throughput for regular parallel work but depend on data movement and memory bandwidth.

en.title: Hardware security and trust
en.short: Threat models, side channels, trojans, secure boot, trusted execution, PUFs and evaluation.

sections.heading: Threat models and trust
sections.text: Hardware security protects a device against attackers who may have physical access, supply-chain access or software access. A threat model states the attacker’s powers, goals and knowledge; for example, a smart meter attacker may read power traces but not modify the chip. Trust means the system behaves as intended despite those powers. A common model separates a trusted computing base, the small part relied on, from untrusted components. Hardware roots of trust are assumed trustworthy, so supply-chain assurance matters.

sections.heading: Side channels and faults
sections.text: Side-channel attacks infer secrets from physical leakage such as timing, power, electromagnetic emission or cache behaviour. Simple power analysis may reveal a sequence of operations; differential power analysis uses many traces and statistics. Fault injection, by voltage or clock glitches or lasers, can skip checks. Countermeasures include constant-time code, masking (randomising intermediate values), hiding (reducing leakage), and redundancy or sensors against faults. These raise cost but are not absolute.

sections.heading: Trojans, boot and TEEs
